issues.legal_issue: A certificate for appeal must show that the High Court judicially considered whether the case is fit for appeal and must disclose its reasons.
material_facts: The High Court’s order stated only that leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was granted.
The order did not certify that the case was fit for appeal or state reasons or identify any issue of outstanding importance.
issues.conclusion: The appeals were not properly certified under Article 134(1)(c), and the Court declined to entertain them as appeals under that provision.
issues.legal_principle: Article 134(1)(c) permits an appeal when the High Court certifies that the case is fit for appeal. The word “certifies” requires judicial consideration, and the order must disclose that consideration and its reasons. Following Nar Singh v. State of U.P., the Supreme Court may examine whether a certificate was rightly granted; a bare grant of leave is insufficient.

predicates.appeal_seeks_certificate_under_discretio: The proceeding seeks an appeal on the basis of a certificate that is granted at the High Court’s discretion.
predicates.certificate_order_gives_no_reasons: The High Court’s order does not explain why the case is fit for appeal or identify the basis for granting the certificate.

issues.definition: When a proceeding seeks a discretionary appeal certificate and the order gives no reasons, the appeal is not properly certified.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may consider whether to exercise its special appellate power even when an appeal is not properly certified under the discretionary certificate route.
material_facts: After holding that the certificate was invalid, the Court considered whether the case was fit for the exercise of its special powers.
One ground raised a legal question about convicting persons for unlawful-assembly offences on the basis of mere presence in the assembly.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the matter under the certificate route but proceeded to consider the case under its special appellate power and found the legal ground concerning mere presence sufficient to do so.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136(1) gives the Supreme Court a discretion to grant special leave to appeal. The invalidity of a certificate under Article 134(1)(c) does not prevent the Court from considering whether to exercise that separate discretion.

predicates.appeal_certificate_is_invalid: The proceeding does not have a valid certificate for an appeal through the discretionary certificate route.
predicates.special_appeal_power_is_invoked: A party asks the Supreme Court to use its separate discretionary power to review the case.
predicates.case_raises_substantial_legal_error: The case raises a significant legal question about whether the lower court applied the law correctly.

issues.definition: Even without a valid certificate, the Supreme Court may review a case under its separate special appellate power when that power is invoked and a substantial legal error is raised.

issues.legal_issue: A suspect or deliberately unreliable police record cannot be used to displace reliable testimony given in court.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on four eyewitnesses whose testimony in court implicated the accused.
The courts below found that the investigating police officer had recorded the witnesses’ statements in a perfunctory or dishonest manner.
The High Court nevertheless acquitted some accused because their names or attributed acts did not appear in that police record.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred by using the unreliable police record to discard evidence given in court; the record’s unreliability reduced its value for testing that evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Statements made to an investigating police officer are not substantive evidence, though they may be used to test the veracity of testimony given in court. When the police record is suspect because it was deliberately perfunctory or dishonest, it loses much of its usual value. The Court applied this principle in assessing the High Court’s reliance on the record; it cited no earlier case for this evidentiary point.

predicates.criminal_appeal_relies_on_witness_testim: The prosecution case in a criminal appeal depends on testimony given by witnesses in court.
predicates.police_record_is_deliberately_unreliable: The record of witnesses’ statements made during police investigation was deliberately incomplete, distorted, or otherwise unreliable.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal depends on witness testimony and the police record is deliberately unreliable, that record cannot displace reliable testimony given in court.

issues.legal_issue: Mere presence in an unlawful assembly does not establish membership unless conduct or a legally recognized circumstance shows that the person joined the assembly.
material_facts: The case involved convictions for offences committed by an unlawful assembly.
The assembly was alleged to have included many residents whose homes surrounded the place of the attack, and the prosecution evidence against some accused was general rather than individualized.

Four appellants had no particular part or overt act attributed to them and might have been spectators; other appellants were linked to specific conduct, including attacking victims, inciting the mob, concealing the crime, or disposing of the bodies.
issues.conclusion: Mere presence was insufficient to establish membership in the unlawful assembly. The four appellants against whom no particular part or overt act was attributed were acquitted, while the convictions of the other appellants were maintained where the evidence showed participation or other conduct supporting membership.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 149 and 142 of the Indian Penal Code, mere presence in an assembly does not make a person a member of an unlawful assembly unless the person does something or omits to do something that makes them a member, or the case falls within Section 142. Evidence in general terms that people were present and armed must be closely scrutinized, and each accused’s case must be considered individually. Conduct connected with disposing of the victims’ bodies could support membership where that conduct furthered the assembly’s common object.

predicates.unlawful_assembly_prosecution: The proceeding involves criminal liability for offences alleged to have been committed by an unlawful assembly.
predicates.accused_presence_is_shown: The evidence places the accused at or among the people assembled at the scene.
predicates.no_individual_conduct_or_other_membershi: The evidence shows no conduct or omission by the accused establishing membership and no legally recognized basis for treating the accused as a member.

issues.definition: In an unlawful-assembly prosecution, presence without individual conduct or another basis for membership does not establish that the accused was a member.
